h1: DC Cable Size for Solar Panels
author: ali-ahmad

fields.name: amps
fields.label: String current
fields.hint: Isc (short-circuit current) of one panel from its label (strings in series carry the same current). If two strings are joined before this cable, add their currents.

fields.name: volts
fields.label: String voltage
fields.hint: Vmp of one panel × panels in series. Higher string voltage means a smaller drop for the same cable.

fields.name: length_m
fields.label: Cable run, one way
fields.hint: Distance from the panels to the inverter or controller along the actual route. The calculator counts both the positive and negative conductor.

fields.name: area_mm2
fields.label: Cable size to check
fields.hint: Pick a size and see its drop. 4 mm² and 6 mm² are the PV cable sizes sold for strings; the larger sizes are for battery-to-inverter runs.

fields.name: circuit
fields.label: Voltage drop limit
fields.hint: Solar DC runs are usually kept under three percent so the panels lose little output; five percent is the general wiring limit.

fields.name: method
fields.label: How the PV cable is laid
options: On the roof, frame or a tray
In free air, spaced from surfaces

fields.name: ambient_c
fields.label: Air temperature around the cable
fields.hint: Air under and around the panels on a summer roof. Solar cable ratings start from hot air; above that the rating is reduced, and this check uses the reduced rating.

fields.name: rho
fields.label: Copper resistivity
fields.hint: Resistance of copper at working temperature. Leave the default for copper PV cable.

outputs.label: Cable current rating on the roof

At {{ex.1.in.length_m|int}} m the same string loses {{ex.1.out.drop_pct|2}}% in 4 mm² and {{ex.2.out.drop_pct|2}}% in 6 mm², so both are within the limit; 6 mm² simply wastes less energy for the life of the system.

String voltage matters more than cable size: the same {{ex.3.in.amps|int}} A over {{ex.3.in.length_m|int}} m at {{ex.3.in.volts|int}} V loses {{ex.3.out.drop_pct|2}}% in 4 mm², over the {{ex.3.out.limit_pct|int}}% limit, while at {{in.volts|int}} V it loses {{out.drop_pct|2}}%.

A battery-to-inverter cable carries far more current: {{ex.4.in.amps|1}} A at {{ex.4.in.volts|int}} V over {{ex.4.in.length_m|int}} m in {{ex.4.in.area_mm2|int}} mm² loses {{ex.4.out.drop_pct|2}}%, which is why battery cables are short and thick.

formula.text: ΔV = 2 × L × I × ρ ÷ A; drop% = ΔV ÷ V_string × 100; V_inverter = V_string − ΔV
lines: L = one-way cable run in metres (the two counts the return conductor)
I = string current in amps (Isc from the panel label; the cable must carry 1.25 × Isc)
ρ = resistivity of copper in Ω·mm²/m at working temperature

sections.h2: How is the DC cable size for solar panels worked out?
p: A solar DC cable has to pass two checks: it must carry the string current safely, and it must not lose too much voltage over the run. For a single string the first check is easy: a string carries only one panel's current, and 4 mm² copper PV cable, the common size for strings, is rated well above the short-circuit current of any common panel with the {{d.margin|2}} safety margin. The second check, voltage drop, is what this calculator does: {{in.amps|int}} A over {{in.length_m|int}} m in {{in.area_mm2|int}} mm² loses {{out.drop_v|1}} V, {{out.drop_pct|2}}% of a {{in.volts|int}} V string.
Pick 4 mm² first. If the drop is above the limit, pick 6 mm² and check again. The table below does this for common runs so you can see where 4 mm² stops being enough.

sections.h2: 4 mm² or 6 mm² solar cable: which one for my run?
p: For a {{in.amps|int}} A string at {{in.volts|int}} V, 4 mm² stays under the {{out.limit_pct|int}}% limit at {{in.length_m|int}} m ({{out.drop_pct|2}}%) and even at {{ex.1.in.length_m|int}} m ({{ex.1.out.drop_pct|2}}%). 6 mm² at {{ex.2.in.length_m|int}} m drops {{ex.2.out.drop_pct|2}}%. On a high-voltage string both pass, so the choice is about lost energy: the drop percentage is also the share of that string's output lost as heat in the cable, every day for twenty-five years, which often pays for 6 mm² on a long run.

On a low-voltage string the answer changes. Three panels in series at {{ex.3.in.volts|int}} V lose {{ex.3.out.drop_pct|2}}% in 4 mm² over {{ex.3.in.length_m|int}} m, above the {{ex.3.out.limit_pct|int}}% limit, so 6 mm² is needed; the table shows the 6 mm² figure. More panels in series is the cheapest fix.

sections.h2: Solar wire size for a five kW inverter
p: A five kW hybrid inverter is usually fed by two strings. Each string on its own cable carries one panel's current and 4 mm² is normal. If the two strings are joined in a combiner before one cable runs to the inverter, that cable carries twice the current; the table includes a two-string case at {{in.volts|int}} V. Cables that carry combined strings must also be checked for current rating: this page warns when the current is above the cable's rating in conduit, but use the wire size calculator in DC mode for the current check, and never combine more strings than the cable and the inverter input allow.
The AC output of the inverter to the distribution board is an ordinary single-phase circuit; size it with the wire size calculator and protect it with the MCB from the breaker size calculator.

sections.h2: Battery cable size for an inverter
p: The cable between the battery and the inverter is the opposite case: low voltage and very high current. A three kW inverter on a {{ex.4.in.volts|int}} V bank draws at least {{ex.4.in.amps|1}} A (more with the inverter's losses and a low battery), and even a {{ex.4.in.length_m|int}} m run in {{ex.4.in.area_mm2|int}} mm² loses {{ex.4.out.drop_pct|2}}%. The size here is set by current rating, not by drop: check it with the wire size calculator in DC mode, which picks the cable from the current table and gives the Pakistani size. Keep battery cables as short as possible and fit a DC-rated fuse or breaker at the battery.

A five kW inverter on 48 V draws over a hundred amps, more than the largest cable in our table carries; the inverter maker's manual gives the cable and fuse for it, and a licensed electrician should fit them.

sections.h2: PV cable sizing: what else to check
p: Use real PV cable (double-insulated, UV-resistant, rated for the DC voltage of the string) with MC4 connectors, not ordinary building wire. Keep the positive and negative close together to limit lightning-induced voltage, route the cable out of direct sun where you can, and fit a DC isolator at the inverter. The string's open-circuit voltage on a cold morning must stay below the inverter's or controller's maximum input voltage; the charge controller size calculator explains that check.

mistakes: Measuring one way and forgetting the return. The current goes out on the positive and back on the negative, so the calculator doubles the run; a straight-line guess also misses the route over the parapet and down the wall.
Using building wire on the roof. Ordinary PVC wire is not rated for sun, rain or the DC voltage of a string; use double-insulated PV cable with MC4 connectors.
Combining strings without checking the current. Two strings on one cable double the amps; the drop doubles and the cable's current rating must be checked separately.
Fixing a drop with thicker cable when more panels in series would do. Raising the string voltage cuts the percentage drop and the cost at the same time, within the inverter's voltage limits.
Going below 4 mm² because the drop allows it. 4 mm² is the common PV cable size for strings and keeps a current margin; this calculator does not offer smaller sizes.
safety: Solar strings carry lethal DC voltage whenever there is daylight and cannot be switched off at the panels; the DC cables, isolators, fuses, earthing and surge protection must be installed by a licensed electrician or a certified solar installer, and the cable's current rating must be confirmed against the combined string current.

faq.q: What size DC cable do I need for solar panels?
faq.a: 4 mm² PV cable for most single strings: a {{in.amps|int}} A string at {{in.volts|int}} V loses only {{out.drop_pct|2}}% over {{in.length_m|int}} m. Move to 6 mm² on long runs or low-voltage strings, and check combined strings for current rating too.

Both carry a single string's current. 4 mm² is enough where the drop stays under the limit: {{ex.1.out.drop_pct|2}}% at {{ex.1.in.length_m|int}} m for a {{ex.1.in.amps|int}} A string at {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} V. 6 mm² cuts that to {{ex.2.out.drop_pct|2}}% and is worth it on long runs or where the string voltage is low.

faq.q: What is an acceptable voltage drop for solar DC cables?
faq.a: Keep it under {{d.vdrop_limit_lighting_pct|int}}% for the string cable; {{d.vdrop_limit_other_pct|int}}% is the general wiring maximum. The percentage lost is energy lost every day, so lower is better where the cable cost is small.

faq.q: Does this calculator pick the cable size for me?
faq.a: It checks the size you pick, and the table shows the common sizes for common runs so you can choose the smallest that passes. It also checks the current against the solar cable's rating on a hot roof and warns when it is above it; to pick the size for combined strings or battery cables use the wire size calculator in DC mode.

faq.q: What cable size between the battery and the inverter?
faq.a: That cable is sized by current, not drop: at least {{ex.4.in.amps|1}} A for a three kW inverter on {{ex.4.in.volts|int}} V, and more when the battery is low and with the inverter's own losses. {{ex.4.in.area_mm2|int}} mm² over {{ex.4.in.length_m|int}} m drops only {{ex.4.out.drop_pct|2}}%, but confirm the current rating with the wire size calculator and the inverter manual.

faq.q: What wire size for a five kW solar inverter?
faq.a: On the DC side each string normally gets 4 mm² PV cable; combined strings need a current check. The AC output is a single-phase circuit sized with the wire size calculator, and a five kW inverter on 48 V draws over a hundred amps from the battery, so follow the maker's cable and fuse table for that run.

faq.q: Why does a low-voltage string need a thicker cable?
faq.a: The volts lost depend on current, length and cable, not on the string voltage, so the same {{ex.3.out.drop_v|1}} V is {{ex.3.out.drop_pct|2}}% of a {{ex.3.in.volts|int}} V string but only {{out.drop_pct|2}}% of a {{in.volts|int}} V string. Adding panels in series is the cheapest cure.
